profile.summary: Akita predicts how a stretch of DNA folds in three dimensions. It takes just over one megabase of sequence, one-hot encoded, and returns a predicted contact map for that window, as log observed over expected values, for each of five cell types it was trained on. It is used for in silico work: saturation mutagenesis, interpreting eQTLs, predicting the effect of structural variants and comparing species.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract (Europe PMC record); params.json: model; targets.txt; explore_model.ipynb

summary_quotes.text: Here we present a convolutional neural network, Akita, that accurately predicts genome folding from DNA sequence alone.
we demonstrate how Akita can be used to perform in silico saturation mutagenesis, interpret eQTLs, make predictions for structural variants and probe species-specific genome folding

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Akita is a convolutional network in two halves. A 1D trunk reads the one-hot sequence: a convolution block, then a tower of ten convolution and pooling blocks, then eight dilated residual blocks, which brings 1,048,576 bases down to 2,048 bp bins. A 2D head turns the 1D representation into a pairwise map (one_to_two with a mean operation), concatenates a distance encoding, symmetrises it, applies six dilated 2D residual blocks, crops the edges and reads off the upper triangle with a diagonal offset of 2. The final layer has five linear units, one per training dataset. Training used mean squared error with SGD, batch size 2, and reverse-complement and shift augmentation. The published model has 751,653 parameters, of which 746,149 are trainable.
sections.source_locator: params.json: model trunk and head_hic, train; keras_print.txt; explore_model.ipynb

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are two generations. The published model is a single TensorFlow checkpoint, model_best.h5, trained on human Hi-C and micro-C mapped to hg38 at 2048 bp resolution, with params.json as its configuration. In 2021 the authors retrained Akita on human and mouse data together after a further hyperparameter search, splitting the genome into eight folds and training one model per held-out fold; those data and models sit in Google Cloud Storage under gs://basenji_hic/3-2021, with model file suffix 0 for human and 1 for mouse. A result should say which generation and, for the 2021 set, which fold and species. This page read the repository at commit 06ce5d38.

facts.value: Supervised convolutional neural network predicting contact maps from DNA sequence.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: 1D trunk (conv block, 10-block conv tower, 8 dilated residual blocks) feeding a 2D head (one_to_two, distance concatenation, symmetrise, 6 dilated 2D residual blocks, crop, upper triangle) with 5 linear output units.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: One-hot encoded DNA of length 1,048,576 bases (2^20), shaped [regions, 1048576, 4].

strengths.text: One forward pass gives maps for five cell types at once, so cell-type differences can be read from the same prediction.

Code, model configuration and a notebook that predicts from an arbitrary sequence are published in the Apache-2.0 Basenji repository, with scripts that download the weights and training data (no licence is stated for those files), and the repository also holds the training scripts.

run_guide.summary: Install Basenji, download the trained Akita model, and predict a contact map for one megabase of hg38 sequence.
prerequisites: Python 3 with the Basenji dependencies from environment.yml or requirements.txt, and TensorFlow installed separately (the README says the codebase works with the latest TensorFlow 2 and should also work with 1.15).
cooltools for the exploration notebook, installed with pip.
pysam and a copy of hg38 (the notebook downloads hg38.ml.fa.gz from basenji_barnyard2 if it is missing).
The notebook sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to -1, so it runs on CPU. GPU memory needs are not stated in the sources read.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit and install it
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/calico/basenji.git
cd basenji
git checkout --detach 06ce5d387e20b47184d05433b3983163c5f923cd
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate basenji
conda install tensorflow
python setup.py develop --no-deps
pip install cooltools

steps.title: Load the model and predict from a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import json, os, subprocess
os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = '-1' ### run on CPU
import numpy as np
import pysam
from basenji import dna_io, seqnn

with open('params.json') as params_open:
    params = json.load(params_open)
    params_model = params['model']

seqnn_model = seqnn.SeqNN(params_model)
seqnn_model.restore('model_best.h5')
print('successfully loaded')

os.makedirs('./data', exist_ok=True)
if not os.path.isfile('./data/hg38.ml.fa'):
    print('downloading hg38.ml.fa')
    subprocess.call('curl -o ./data/hg38.ml.fa.gz https://storage.googleapis.com/basenji_barnyard2/hg38.ml.fa.gz', shell=True)
    subprocess.call('gunzip ./data/hg38.ml.fa.gz', shell=True)

fasta_open = pysam.Fastafile('./data/hg38.ml.fa')
seq = fasta_open.fetch('chr12', 115163136, 116211712).upper()
seq_1hot = dna_io.dna_1hot(seq)
test_pred_from_seq = seqnn_model.model.predict(np.expand_dims(seq_1hot,0))
print(test_pred_from_seq.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The notebook's cells for loading the model and predicting from sequence, stitched into one shell heredoc. The region chr12:115163136-116211712 is one of the notebook's own example test regions, which is 2^20 bases long. The makedirs line and the final print of the output shape are additions.

Two generations exist and the second (2021, human plus mouse, eight folds) is documented only by a short README in manuscripts/akita/v2; a benchmark result should say which was used.
